result.party_text: The RAD’s three-person panel decided the appeal in a May 17, 2017 split Decision, with both majority and minority upholding the RPD’s refusal but under different frameworks and reasons.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD panel's split decision with majority and minority upholding the RPD refusal under different frameworks.

result.party_text: The RAD majority held that the RAD owes deference to the RPD’s credibility findings in some situations where the RPD has a meaningful advantage, and will not interfere if the RPD’s reasoning was comprehensible and based on evidence.
result.why: The court summarizes the RAD majority's view on deference to RPD credibility findings and conditions for non-interference.

result.party_text: The RAD majority’s framework on when there is a meaningful advantage and the concept of RAD reasonableness is problematic.
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicant's point that the RAD majority's framework on meaningful advantage and reasonableness is problematic.

result.party_text: Applying its framework, the RAD majority dismissed the family’s appeal.
result.why: The court states that the RAD majority applied its framework and dismissed the family's appeal.

result.party_text: The RAD minority also dismissed the appeal but disagreed with the majority’s framework and limits on the RAD’s authority to intervene in RPD decisions.
result.why: The court notes the RAD minority also dismissed the appeal but disagreed with the majority's framework and limits on RAD authority.

result.party_text: The RAD erred in applying a deferential standard of review when the RPD had a meaningful advantage in making a finding, and erred in dismissing the Applicants' appeal under that framework.
result.answer_quote: It is clear that the first issue is reviewable on a reasonableness standard because it involves the interpretation of IRPA, the RAD’s home statute (Huruglica at para 30). This gives rise to a presumption of reasonableness, which has not been rebutted here (Williams Lake Indian Band v Canada (Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development), 2018 SCC 4 at para 138; Barreau du Québec v Quebec (Attorney General), 2017 SCC 56 at para 15). The second issue of whether the RAD’s Decision was reasonable in light of the answer to the first question is also reviewable on a reasonableness standard, since it involves a matter of mixed fact and law (Huruglica at para 35).
result.why: The court applies a reasonableness standard and finds no error in the RAD's approach, rejecting the applicant's claim of error.

result.party_text: The RAD majority found it should show deference to some RPD findings in specific cases, based primarily on two observations: credibility is normally determined on oral hearing, and the RPD generally has a better position and expertise to make credibility findings than the RAD, which rarely holds oral hearings.
result.answer_quote: The RAD majority based this conclusion primarily on two observations. The majority relied, in part on what it described as “the seminal Singh decision” (Singh v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1985] 1 SCR 177), which found, regarding credibility findings made solely on the basis of written submissions:
result.why: The court recounts the RAD majority's reasoning for deference to some RPD findings based on oral hearing and expertise.

result.party_text: The Minister argues that the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica decided that the RAD must apply a deferential standard of review to some RPD credibility findings where it has a meaningful advantage.
result.why: The court states the Minister's argument that Huruglica decided RAD must apply deferential review to some RPD credibility findings.

result.party_text: The interveners CARL/CCR argue that IRPA's relevant sections allow only one standard of review for all factual findings: correctness, and that Huruglica's comments on deference refer only to the RAD's remedial power, not the substantive review lens.
result.why: The court presents CARL/CCR's argument that IRPA allows only correctness standard and Huruglica's deference comments relate only to remedial power.

result.party_text: The Applicants submit that the RAD must review all findings for correctness but allow a limited role for deference alongside correctness review.
result.why: The court notes the Applicants' submission that RAD must review all findings for correctness but allow limited deference.

result.party_text: The third intervener, AQAADI, shares the Applicants' view that deference is more theoretical than real for the RAD due to the nature of IRPA and that deference is almost never justified.
result.why: The court records AQAADI's view that deference is theoretical and almost never justified due to IRPA's nature.

result.party_text: The controversy is about how to interpret Huruglica's comments on the RAD's standard of review in RPD appeals, specifically whether the RAD should apply correctness to determine if the RPD erred beyond just reviewing reasonableness of findings of fact.
result.why: The court explains the controversy about Huruglica's comments on RAD's standard of review and the Federal Court of Appeal's reformulation.

result.party_text: The Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD must apply the correctness standard to determine whether the RPD erred, based on the purpose and object of IRPA and the legislative scheme under sections 110 and 111.
result.why: The court confirms the Federal Court of Appeal held the RAD must apply correctness standard based on IRPA's purpose and sections 110 and 111.

result.party_text: The Federal Court of Appeal made observations about section 111(2)(b) of IRPA empowering the RAD to refer cases back to the RPD when it cannot confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence.
result.why: The court reproduces the Federal Court of Appeal's observations about section 111(2)(b) empowering the RAD to refer cases back to the RPD.

result.party_text: The Minister argues that the Federal Court of Appeal focused on the RPD's factual findings relating to credibility and excluded such findings from the correctness standard, ruling that correctness is not appropriate for credibility findings.
result.why: The court acknowledges the Minister's argument that the Federal Court of Appeal excluded credibility findings from the correctness standard.

result.party_text: The Minister argues that credibility findings are central to Huruglica and not incidental comments, based on the Federal Court of Appeal's observations about the RPD's fact-finding advantage.
result.why: The court records the Minister's argument that credibility findings are central to Huruglica and not incidental comments.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that the Minister's view misreads Huruglica, stating that the Federal Court of Appeal's comments on deference relate only to the RAD's choice of remedy, not its review for error.
result.why: The court notes CARL/CCR's argument that the Minister misreads Huruglica, which relates deference only to remedy choice, not error review.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR explain that the RAD's inquisitorial process means it plays a more active role than the RPD, which is adversarial, citing Benitez v Canada for the distinction.
result.why: The court explains CARL/CCR's explanation of the RAD's inquisitorial role versus the RPD's adversarial role, citing Benitez.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that the Federal Court of Appeal's mention of the RPD's meaningful advantage refers to the RPD's ability to shape the inquisitorial record through oral hearings, which the RAD cannot do, and that the RAD wrongly concluded the RPD has an advantage in interpreting the record.
result.why: The court restates and accepts CARL/CCR's argument about the RPD's advantage being due to oral hearings and the RAD's incorrect conclusion.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that Huruglica's comments on deference relate solely to the RAD's remedial powers under section 111 of IRPA and are unrelated to the standard of review.
result.why: The court accepts CARL/CCR's argument that Huruglica's comments on deference relate only to remedial powers, not standard of review.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that the plain language of IRPA and the Federal Court of Appeal's statutory analysis in Huruglica require the RAD to apply a correctness standard to all RPD findings, including credibility.
result.why: The court accepts CARL/CCR's argument that IRPA and Huruglica require the RAD to apply correctness standard to all RPD findings.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that the RAD has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all questions of fact under subsection 162(1) of IRPA, may hear appeals on questions of fact under subsection 110(1), and must confirm, substitute, or refer back RPD determinations under subsection 111(1) and (2), and that Huruglica empowers the RAD to review all RPD findings for correctness.
result.why: The court accepts CARL/CCR's argument about RAD's exclusive jurisdiction and powers under IRPA and Huruglica to review all RPD findings for correctness.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that a correctness review of all RPD findings is supported by the RAD's legislative purpose, noting that before the RAD's creation two RPD members decided each refugee claim and the RAD was meant to improve efficiency without reducing the safety net of independent decisions by two members.
result.why: The court accepts CARL/CCR's argument that correctness review is supported by RAD's legislative purpose and history.

result.party_text: The Applicants agree with CARL/CCR that IRPA unambiguously requires a correctness review for all findings of fact, emphasizing that Huruglica equated 'wrong' with correctness review and that it would make no sense to interpret 'wrong' differently depending on the nature of the factual finding.
result.why: The court accepts the Applicants' agreement with CARL/CCR that IRPA requires correctness review for all findings of fact.

result.party_text: Unlike CARL/CCR, the Applicants acknowledge Huruglica envisioned a role for deference, but argue that the RAD should show deference as restraint before applying a correctness standard, with deference only outside the ambit of standard of review.
result.answer_quote: With respect to the Applicants’ position that deference can co-exist with a correctness review of all factual findings, I do not agree. Rather, correctness as a standard of review is defined by the absence of deference (Dunsmuir at para 34). In Maritime Broadcasting System Limited v Canadian Media Guild, 2014 FCA 59, the Federal Court of Appeal wrote: “[c]orrectness review has always been review without any deference. ‘Correctness with a degree of deference’ is a non-sequitur. It would be like describing a car as stationary but moving” (at para 60). With this image in mind, the materials before me do not reflect that the Federal Court of Appeal envisioned a role for deference in the manner suggested by the Applicants. As a result, I am not persuaded by the Applicants’ argument that the RAD must apply a single correctness review to all of the RPD’s findings, and defer by showing restraint before applying correctness – even though I recognize that Huruglica at paragraph 70 (reproduced above) mentioned a degree of restraint twice.
result.why: Court rejects the argument that RAD should show deference before applying correctness, stating correctness means no deference.

result.party_text: The Applicants suggest that deference is understood as reasonableness and giving of weight, citing Professor Daly's theories of doctrinal and epistemic deference.
result.answer_quote: Finally, I do not find any merit to the sources that the Applicants rely upon, namely Re: Sound, and Professor Daly’s views of doctrinal or epistemic deference.
result.why: Court finds no merit in the Applicants' reliance on Professor Daly's theories of deference.

result.party_text: The Applicants refer to the Federal Court of Appeal's analysis in Re: Sound v Fitness Industry Council of Canada as supporting their approach to correctness with deference, and argue that the RAD minority approach appropriately envisions a role for deference alongside correctness review.
result.answer_quote: Finally, I do not find any merit to the sources that the Applicants rely upon, namely Re: Sound, and Professor Daly’s views of doctrinal or epistemic deference.
result.why: Court rejects the Applicants' reliance on Re: Sound as supporting correctness with deference.

result.party_text: The Federal Court of Appeal observed that problems arise when the RPD's credibility findings themselves are challenged before the RAD, as noted in Huruglica at paragraph 72.
result.why: Court acknowledges the Federal Court of Appeal's observation about problems when RPD's credibility findings are challenged before RAD.

result.party_text: The Federal Court of Appeal made general statutory observations on paragraph 111(2)(b) of IRPA in Huruglica.
result.answer_quote: Subject to my comments with respect to paragraph 111(2)(b), I generally agree with the RAD’s finding that neither section 110 nor 111, nor the legislation as a whole, point to the need to show deference to the RPD’s findings of fact.
result.why: Court notes the Federal Court of Appeal's general statutory observations on paragraph 111(2)(b) of IRPA and agrees with RAD's finding on deference.

result.party_text: The Applicants rely on Re: Sound and Professor Daly’s views of doctrinal or epistemic deference.
result.why: Court rejects the Applicants' reliance on Re: Sound and Professor Daly's views.

result.party_text: The RAD found that neither section 110 nor 111, nor the legislation as a whole, point to the need to show deference to the RPD’s findings of fact.
result.why: The court agrees with the RAD's finding that the legislation does not require deference to RPD's findings of fact.

result.party_text: The RAD acknowledged that the provisions evidence the legislator’s intent that the RAD bring finality to the refugee claims determination process.
result.why: The court acknowledges that the provisions show the legislator's intent for RAD to bring finality to refugee claims.

result.party_text: The RAD majority concluded that under IRPA it should apply two standards of review to RPD findings: correctness in most cases and deference on occasion.
result.answer_quote: To the contrary, given the statutory analysis in Huruglica, this was clearly an outcome open to the RAD.
result.why: The court finds it reasonable that the RAD applies two standards of review: correctness generally and deference occasionally.

result.party_text: The question arises when deference should be triggered in reviewing RPD findings.
result.why: The court states the question of when deference should be triggered but does not answer it here.

result.party_text: The second question is whether the RAD majority reasonably set out the conditions triggering the application of a deferential standard of review.
result.why: The court frames the question about whether the RAD reasonably set out conditions for deference but does not answer it here.

result.party_text: For any given RPD finding, the RAD must decide when to apply a correctness standard and when to apply a deferential standard.
result.why: The court restates the question about when to apply correctness or deference but does not answer it here.

result.party_text: The question arises when deference applies to the RAD.
result.answer_quote: The RAD, of course, is distinct from an appellate court, and thus many of the justifications for the deferential standard outlined in Housen (including respect for the integrity of the trial process and judicial economy) do not apply. I turn to its Decision to consider its findings on this key question under review today. In the Decision, the RAD majority decided, based on its reading of Huruglica, that a deferential standard was only appropriate where the RPD truly had a meaningful advantage in making the finding at issue. The RAD majority held that such a determination must be made on a case-by-case basis and, where the RAD concludes that a meaningful advantage existed, it must explain why. It further indicates that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim.
result.why: The court explains when deference applies to the RAD, emphasizing case-by-case analysis and meaningful advantage.

result.party_text: The RAD majority set out eight categories of RPD credibility findings as guidelines for future panels: inconsistencies, contradictions and omissions; demeanour; specialized knowledge; relevant knowledge; implausibilities; inferences; documents; and oral hearing.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD majority set out eight categories of RPD credibility findings as guidelines.

result.party_text: The RAD majority explained the context for each of these eight categories, some of which did not arise on the facts of this case.
result.why: The court notes the RAD majority explained the context for each category, some not arising in this case.

result.party_text: The RAD majority reviewed when it might be at a disadvantage, and thus owe deference to the RPD for each of the eight categories.
result.why: The court states the RAD majority reviewed when it might owe deference to the RPD for each category.

result.party_text: The RPD may have a meaningful advantage in assessing inconsistencies, contradictions, and omissions in oral testimony because the RPD sees and hears the witness, chooses which questions to ask, and listens to the answers.
result.why: The court accepts that the RPD may have a meaningful advantage in assessing inconsistencies, contradictions, and omissions in oral testimony.

result.party_text: Paragraph 111(2)(b) provides that once an error has been identified, the RAD may refer the matter back for redetermination only if it cannot make a decision confirming or setting aside the RPD decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD.
result.why: The court explains paragraph 111(2)(b) about when the RAD may refer back for redetermination after an error is identified.

result.party_text: In some cases where oral testimony is critical or determinative, the RAD may not be in a position to confirm or substitute its own determination to that of the RPD.
result.why: The court accepts that in some cases oral testimony is critical and the RAD may not be able to substitute its own determination.

result.party_text: There may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law because they require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears.
result.why: The court accepts that the RPD may have a meaningful advantage in assessing credibility or weight of oral evidence.

result.party_text: The RAD should sometimes exercise restraint before substituting its own determination, but whether such restraint is warranted should be addressed case-by-case.
result.why: The court agrees that restraint by the RAD should be exercised case-by-case.

result.party_text: The RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision on the refugee claim.
result.why: The court accepts that the RAD should determine if the RPD had an advantage and if it can still decide the claim.

result.party_text: When the RPD finds a witness straightforward and credible, there is no issue of credibility per se, and the RAD can rely on the RPD’s findings to reach a conclusion.
result.why: The court accepts that if the RPD finds a witness credible, the RAD can rely on that to reach a conclusion.

result.party_text: Problems occur when credibility findings themselves are disputed on appeal and the RAD cannot reach a conclusion without endorsing or rejecting those findings.
result.why: The court accepts that problems arise when credibility findings are disputed and the RAD cannot decide without endorsing or rejecting them.

result.party_text: If the RAD can identify an error in credibility findings based on plausibility, the RPD may have no real advantage over the RAD.
result.why: Court agrees RAD may have no advantage if error in credibility based on plausibility is identified.

result.party_text: If a finding that a witness is not credible was based on discrepancies that could not justify such a conclusion or that did not exist, and the RAD can easily identify the error, the RAD may refer back to the RPD with directions.
result.why: Court agrees RAD can refer back if credibility errors based on discrepancies are easily identified.

result.party_text: It is not appropriate to say more about various scenarios that may arise; the RAD should develop its own jurisprudence and is not pigeon-holed to a level of deference in each case.
result.why: Court declines to elaborate and says RAD should develop its own jurisprudence.

result.party_text: The RAD majority erred in pre-emptively establishing categories of credibility findings warranting deference instead of determining meaningful advantage case-by-case.
result.why: Court states applicants argue RAD erred, but does not accept this argument here.

result.party_text: The RAD established an unreasonably rigid approach ignoring many possible permutations and unique situations, separating meaningful advantage from the circumstances of the particular hearing.
result.why: Court notes applicants' submission but does not accept the claim of unreasonably rigid approach.

result.party_text: Under the RAD’s model, whether a meaningful advantage exists seems to turn almost entirely on whether the finding arose from oral evidence, leading to an unreasonably broad band of deference.
result.why: Court records applicants' argument but does not accept that RAD's model leads to unreasonably broad deference.

result.party_text: The RAD has failed to conduct a case-by-case analysis and has been overly deferential when RPD credibility findings were based on oral testimony.
result.why: The court accepts the intervener's point that the RAD failed to conduct case-by-case analysis and was overly deferential to RPD credibility findings based on oral testimony.

result.party_text: The RAD majority did not err in setting out categories for meaningful advantage and made clear that the inquiry must be done in every case.
result.why: The court rejects the respondent's claim that the RAD majority did not err in setting out categories and requiring meaningful advantage inquiry in every case.

result.party_text: The RAD was illustrating situations where the RPD was more likely to have a meaningful advantage.
result.why: The court accepts the respondent's explanation that the RAD was illustrating situations where the RPD was more likely to have a meaningful advantage.

result.party_text: The RPD’s meaningful advantage generally derives from holding an oral hearing where it can observe testimonial evidence.
result.why: The court accepts the respondent's point that the RPD's meaningful advantage generally derives from holding an oral hearing where it can observe testimonial evidence.

result.party_text: If future RAD panels misinterpret the guidance and are overly deferential, this can be corrected on judicial review.
result.why: The court acknowledges the respondent's point that future misinterpretations can be corrected on review but also finds the RAD majority's model unreasonable.

result.party_text: Not all legal theories can be reduced to simple slogans, so the RAD majority’s approach should be accepted.
result.why: The court rejects the respondent's argument that the RAD majority's approach should be accepted despite lack of principled framework.

result.party_text: The RAD majority found meaningful advantage just because the RPD chose questions and saw and heard witnesses, without explaining why this should always trigger deference.
result.why: The court acknowledges the RAD majority found meaningful advantage solely because the RPD saw and heard witnesses without explaining why this always triggers deference.

result.party_text: A concrete way to determine meaningful advantage is to see if the basis for the impugned finding is disclosed in the record before the RAD.
result.why: The court agrees that checking if the basis for the finding is in the record before the RAD is a concrete way to determine meaningful advantage.

result.party_text: The concept of the RPD’s meaningful advantage turns on information to which the RAD does not have access.
result.why: The court records the respondent's position that meaningful advantage depends on information unavailable to the RAD.

result.party_text: The RPD may make credibility findings based on events or circumstances not captured in the hearing recording or transcript, giving it a meaningful advantage.
result.why: The court accepts that the RPD may have meaningful advantage based on events not captured in the hearing record.

result.party_text: The RAD has adopted the applicants' preferred approach in some decisions after the one under review.
result.why: The court notes the applicants' preferred approach has been adopted by the RAD in later decisions.

result.party_text: In X (Re), 2017 CanLII 142903 (CA IRB), the RAD found no meaningful advantage because the errors raised in the appeal pertained to obvious inconsistencies and discrepancies.
result.why: The court notes the RAD found no meaningful advantage in X (Re) because errors were obvious inconsistencies.

result.party_text: The RAD member held, referencing Huruglica and the majority in the RAD Decision, that there was no meaningful advantage.
result.why: The court quotes the RAD member holding no meaningful advantage, referencing Huruglica and the majority in the RAD Decision.

result.party_text: In X (Re), 2017 CanLII 61324 (CA IRB), the RAD member held that the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage because the issues related to the substance of the testimony and not to any behavioural or other item that the RPD could observe and the RAD could not.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD member's holding that the RPD had no meaningful advantage due to the nature of the issues.

result.party_text: In X (Re), 2017 CanLII 142477 (CA IRB), the RAD panel held that, because it had listened to the recording of the hearing and read the RPD’s conclusions, no meaningful advantage existed.
result.why: The court notes the RAD panel's holding that no meaningful advantage existed after listening to the recording and reading conclusions.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR dispute that the RAD is not always in as good a position as the RPD to make factual findings and argue that the RAD is always in as good a position to make factual findings as the RPD.
result.answer_quote: I do not find this comparison useful. The RAD does not perform a de novo review but is constrained by the record before it and its appellate function (Huruglica at paras 79, 103). Rather, I agree with the Applicants that because it is not the RAD’s role to carry out a de novo consideration of the claim, the RAD is tethered to the RPD’s decision (see, for instance, Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v Gebrewold, 2018 FC 374 at para 25).
result.why: The court rejects the argument that the RAD is always as well placed as the RPD, emphasizing the RAD's appellate role and constraints.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that information that a witness intends to convey must always be put into the record by the RPD.
result.why: The text states the argument but does not respond to it.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR cite the possibility of using a video of a witness performing a religious exercise, or a precise description of a questionable conduct issue, such as looking to counsel for answers when asked a question, as examples of information that must be recorded.
result.why: The text states the argument but does not respond to it.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR contend that to the extent the record is deficient, whether by way of non-verbal or physical cues that raise doubts and lead to negative credibility findings, these should be explained clearly and in unmistakeable terms by the decision-maker, who must ensure that the record is clear.
result.why: The text states the argument but does not respond to it.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR argue that demeanour can never reasonably form the basis of a credibility finding.
result.why: The text states the argument but does not respond to it.

result.party_text: Demeanour only has relevance to the fact-finding process to the extent that it facilitates the RPD’s inquisitorial function by alerting the RPD to useful lines of questioning and by allowing it to draw out content that can then be seen in the record and reviewed by the RAD.
result.why: The text states the argument but does not respond to it.

result.party_text: Under IRPA’s statutory scheme, the RAD is meant to function as a second risk assessment on the merits of each claim, and the RAD must do this job even if the evidence before it is imperfect.
result.answer_quote: The RAD does not perform a de novo review but is constrained by the record before it and its appellate function (Huruglica at paras 79, 103). Rather, I agree with the Applicants that because it is not the RAD’s role to carry out a de novo consideration of the claim, the RAD is tethered to the RPD’s decision (see, for instance, Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v Gebrewold, 2018 FC 374 at para 25).
result.why: The court rejects that RAD functions as a second risk assessment and states RAD is tethered to RPD's decision, not a de novo review.

result.party_text: The RPD makes its findings based on imperfect evidence, which may include hearsay or affidavits from individuals not subject to cross-examination.
result.answer_quote: The RAD does not perform a de novo review but is constrained by the record before it and its appellate function (Huruglica at paras 79, 103). Rather, I agree with the Applicants that because it is not the RAD’s role to carry out a de novo consideration of the claim, the RAD is tethered to the RPD’s decision (see, for instance, Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v Gebrewold, 2018 FC 374 at para 25).
result.why: The court rejects the comparison, emphasizing RAD's constrained appellate role rather than independent fact-finding on imperfect evidence.

result.party_text: AQAADI argues strongly against the relevance of demeanour evidence, referring to cases expressing serious concerns regarding its use.
result.why: The court acknowledges AQAADI's strong argument against the relevance of demeanour evidence citing serious concerns.

result.party_text: AQAADI states that in their research they could not find one RAD case where demeanour was the determinative reason for credibility concerns.
result.why: The court notes AQAADI's statement that no RAD case was found where demeanour was determinative for credibility.

result.party_text: AQAADI would not close the door to the possibility that the RPD may, in some cases, have a meaningful advantage, and stresses that the meaningful advantage inquiry must be properly undertaken in every case.
result.why: The court accepts AQAADI's position that the meaningful advantage inquiry must be properly undertaken in every case.

result.party_text: While demeanour evidence has shortcomings, its use remains permissible under Canadian law, and fact-finding is a difficult and complex process to which demeanour has some relevance.
result.answer_quote: However, I have not been persuaded to depart from the views of higher courts as well as a long line of jurisprudence from my Federal Court colleagues, that seeing and hearing a witness may confer a fact-finding advantage to the RPD (see, for instance, Paye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 685 at para 14 with respect to the RAD and Rahal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 319 at paras 41–45). This type of thinking is reasonable and underpins deference to factual findings in other areas of law.
result.why: The court acknowledges demeanour evidence's shortcomings but upholds its permissibility and fact-finding relevance, supporting RPD's advantage.

result.party_text: The interveners urge to distinguish the case law on demeanour evidence due to the unique context of refugee determinations, noting studies and literature that question credibility determinations.
result.why: The court acknowledges the interveners' urging and the literature questioning credibility determinations.

result.party_text: The RAD majority had concerns about its inability to truly review, on a correctness standard, findings based on the RPD’s proximity to a witness and elements that could not be translated into the record.
result.why: The court agrees the RAD majority had concerns about reviewing findings based on RPD's proximity to witnesses.

result.party_text: The RAD majority failed to outline when the RPD's general fact-finding advantage becomes a specific, meaningful advantage justifying a deferential standard of review.
result.why: The court finds the RAD majority failed to outline when RPD's advantage justifies deference.

result.party_text: IRPA integrates institutional deference because a claimant cannot appeal to the RAD if the RPD finds their claim manifestly unfounded or without credible basis.
result.why: The court notes the applicant's argument about IRPA integrating institutional deference.

result.party_text: CARL/CCR focus on remedial deference, where the RAD remits a matter to the RPD instead of substituting its own determination.
result.why: The court acknowledges the respondent's focus on remedial deference where RAD remits matters to RPD.

result.party_text: The RAD majority referred to conflicting case law on whether a reasonableness standard should be used when reviewing RPD credibility findings.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD majority referred to conflicting case law on reasonableness standard for RPD credibility findings.

result.party_text: The RAD majority concluded that the level of deference to RPD credibility findings is not the same as on judicial review because the RAD must independently review the evidence.
result.why: The court restates and accepts the RAD majority's conclusion about the level of deference and independent review.

result.party_text: The RAD majority adopted a standard of RAD reasonableness where the RPD has a meaningful advantage in making credibility findings, relying on judicial review reasonableness jurisprudence.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD majority's adoption of RAD reasonableness and reliance on judicial review jurisprudence.

result.party_text: The RAD majority applied Dunsmuir to assess both process and outcome, requiring the RPD's finding to be comprehensible and supported by evidence.
result.why: The court accepts that the RAD majority applied Dunsmuir to assess process and outcome of RPD findings.

result.party_text: The RAD majority implicitly held that a reasonableness standard could be used if the RAD also conducted an independent assessment.
result.why: The court acknowledges the RAD majority's implicit view on reasonableness standard with independent assessment.

result.party_text: The Applicants argue that RAD reasonableness is unreasonable because it duplicates the Dunsmuir framework at the administrative level.
result.why: The court records the Applicants' argument that RAD reasonableness duplicates Dunsmuir at the administrative level.

result.party_text: The Applicants say RAD reasonableness is contrary to Huruglica, which held that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions like a judicial review.
result.why: The court notes the Applicants' argument that RAD reasonableness conflicts with Huruglica's holding.

result.party_text: The RAD majority's approach results in a situation of 'double deference', where the Federal Court reviews the reasonableness of the RAD's own reasonableness analysis.
result.why: The court acknowledges the applicants' argument about 'double deference' as described in the cited academic source.

result.party_text: Any expression of deference by the RAD should be less than in a reasonableness review and should not use the language of judicial review, as supported by the statutory scheme in IRPA.
result.why: The court records the applicants' argument that RAD's deference should be less and not use judicial review language, supported by IRPA.

result.party_text: The RAD is a highly specialized tribunal itself, not a typical generalist appeal tribunal lacking the specialized expertise of the lower tribunal.
result.why: The court notes the applicants' reliance on Professor Daly's analysis that RAD is a highly specialized tribunal.

result.party_text: RAD reasonableness is distinct from judicial review because the RAD must begin with an overall, independent assessment of the matter, while judicial review focuses on the decision-maker's reasons.
result.why: The court states the Minister's argument that RAD reasonableness is distinct from judicial review due to its independent assessment role.

result.party_text: RAD reasonableness is a term used by the RAD with built-in flexibility appropriate to the level of deference the RAD should give to the RPD, and is thus reasonable.
result.why: The court records the Minister's submission that RAD reasonableness is a flexible term appropriate to the level of deference.

result.party_text: The RAD cannot independently assess the basis for a finding while reviewing it on a deferential standard, creating a fundamental tension between deferential review and the RAD's duty to conduct an independent assessment.
result.why: The court acknowledges the intervener's argument about the tension between deferential review and independent assessment by RAD.

result.party_text: This tension is apparent in the RAD minority's reasoning where the single member warned about the independent assessment obligation.
result.why: The court acknowledges the intervener's point about tension in the RAD minority's reasoning.

result.party_text: The RAD is obligated to undertake an independent assessment, which has been endorsed as a thorough, comprehensive, and independent review by the RAD in subsequent cases following Huruglica.
result.why: The court confirms the RAD's obligation to undertake an independent assessment endorsed by subsequent cases.

result.party_text: An independent assessment could be seen as antithetical to reasonableness review and synonymous with correctness review.
result.answer_quote: I agree with CARL/CCR that, if an independent assessment is understood as equating to correctness, the RAD majority could not reasonably marry this concept with deference. But this Court has also held that even a deferential review by the RAD involves an independent assessment of the evidence (see Guo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 317 at paras 15–19; Jeyaseelan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 278 at paras 19–21). What I take from the above case law is that, for most of the RPD’s findings, the RAD is required to conduct a correctness review and substitute its own conclusions where they differ from those of the RPD. But even for those findings that attract a deferential review, an independent assessment of some form is also needed. Deference never equates to blind endorsement (see Dunsmuir at para 48).
result.why: The court agrees independent assessment can seem antithetical to reasonableness but clarifies it can coexist with deferential review.

result.party_text: The Minister argues that there was no error in the RAD majority using the term reasonableness, as it is just a label describing a level of deference and can be used outside the judicial review context.
result.answer_quote: I think it is obvious here that, regardless of the label it chose, the content of the deferential standard adopted by the RAD majority is duplicative of the framework to be applied on judicial review. In my view, the RAD majority’s conclusions on the content of its deferential standard are not consistent with the Federal Court of Appeal’s instructions that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions in the manner of a judicial review (Huruglica at paras 37, 47–48). I disagree. The Federal Court of Appeal, after reviewing the purposes of the governing legislation, held at paragraph 66 of Huruglica that the RAD is a sui generis statutory body whose role is to act as a safety net.
result.why: The court finds the RAD majority's use of reasonableness duplicates judicial review, which is inconsistent with instructions.
